_why: The ADR's table is a single row, and it is the most interesting kind:
the mutation was not chosen, it HAPPENED. A concurrent agent's mutation
loop restored scripts/report_lab.py from a snapshot taken before my
import line existed. The call site survived; the import did not.
That is worse than a syntax error because nothing notices it -- the
module still imports cleanly, and a source-text check for
`ec_number_for_name` still passes, because the name is right there at
the call site. Only running the branch finds it.
test: cd Tests && python3 -m pytest test_a_name_reaches_every_command.py -q --no-header -p no:cacheprovider

mutations.description: the shared name->EC policy is called without being imported
mutations._note: Verified by hand on a copy before this set existed: the module still imports, and the branch raises `NameError: name 'EnzymeNameNotResolved' is not defined`. The source-level assertion for `from enzyme_lookup import` exists to say WHICH line is missing; this is the one that proves the code runs.
mutations.find: from enzyme_lookup import EnzymeNameNotResolved, ec_number_for_name  # noqa: E402

mutations.description: an ambiguous enzyme name silently resolves to the first candidate
mutations._note: The defect ADR 0126 fixed for `catalog`, restored at the shared policy so it would reach `report` too. 1.1.1.27 is L-lactate dehydrogenase and 1.1.1.28 is D-: a wrong EC is a correctly formatted citation for a different protein.

mutations.description: a network failure is reported as an unknown enzyme
mutations._note: The three-state rule at the name step. 'UniProt has no such enzyme' and 'UniProt could not be reached' send a student to opposite places; collapsing them tells someone their enzyme does not exist because the wifi dropped.
